McLaren: McLaren has tweaked the aerodynamics – a reshaped rear‑wing endplate and new front‑corner and rear‑corner parts – to smooth airflow and give the car a steadier grip through high‑speed corners. They've also added a fresh floor panel and boosted brake‑cooling capacity, which means more consistent downforce and less risk of overheating on this weekend’s track. The result should be a sharper, more stable car that can push harder for laps and defend better in the midfield battle.
Mercedes F1 Team: Mercedes has added a small winglet on the centreline of the rear wing and widened the rear‑exit bodywork to improve airflow and cooling for this circuit’s high‑speed corners. They also merged the tail winglet into the rear‑wing brace, giving the car a cleaner rear end and more stable downforce. The tweaks should boost straight‑line speed while keeping the car stable through fast sections, giving the team a better shot at strong qualifying and race pace this weekend.
Red Bull Racing: Red Bull has tweaked the shape of the rear‑wing pylons, the rear‑wing flap and the diffuser’s underside to tighten up airflow and boost down‑force where it counts most. In plain terms, the car should stick to the tarmac better in high‑speed corners, giving the drivers more grip and stability. Those refinements could translate into stronger cornering performance and a better chance to defend or attack during this weekend’s qualifying and race.
Scuderia Ferrari: Ferrari have reshaped the rear wing – new flap profiles, extra trailing‑edge bits and a re‑contoured end‑plate with fresh pillars – plus an optional winglet tucked into the SM‑fairing. In plain terms, the package gives the team a more flexible way to dial‑in rear down‑force and stability, especially through the high‑speed corners of this weekend’s track. The extra grip should help the car stay on the limit longer and manage tyre wear, giving Ferrari a better shot at defending or attacking on the straight‑line and corner exits.
Williams Racing: Williams has rolled out a circuit‑specific rear‑wing set‑up and a fresh floor layout, each with a reshaped flap and a new winglet on the side of the floor. The tweaks let the car dial down drag on the straights while still keeping enough grip through the corners, giving the team a better balance for the weekend’s track. In short, it should translate into higher top‑end speed without sacrificing the handling needed to stay competitive.
Racing Bulls / RB: Racing Bulls have added tiny winglets to the roll‑hoop, tweaking the airflow to give a bit more rear‑end grip as the car pushes through the corners. The rear‑wing’s support pods and auxiliary pieces have been reshaped for a more consistent load, sharpening stability on the straights and into heavy braking zones. Finally, they’ve introduced new body‑work cooling louvres that can be swapped for the specific temperature demands of this circuit, helping the power unit stay in its optimal temperature window throughout the weekend.
Aston Martin: Aston Martin has reshaped almost the whole aero package – a slimmer, longer nose and a re‑profiled front wing with new endplates push more air to the car’s centre, while the floor, leading‑edge vanes and diffuser have been re‑contoured to recover down‑force lost on the straights. The side‑pod inlet, engine cover and cooling louvers get a tighter shape, and the rear wing now has a re‑balanced chord and added winglets to boost rear grip without adding drag. In short, the car should be stickier through the high‑speed corners of this weekend’s circuit, giving the team a better chance to attack rivals on both the bends and the long‑run straight‑line pace.
Haas F1 Team: Haas has refined the rear‑wing package, reshaping the SM fairing and fitting a new gurney‑flap to tighten the airflow. The tweaks give the car a bit more rear grip without adding drag, helping drivers brake later and corner more confidently. Expect a smoother, more stable feel on the high‑speed sections of this weekend’s track.
Audi F1 Team: Audi’s latest tweak reshapes the rear‑wing endplates to smooth the air that passes over the wing. The cleaner flow gives the car a bit more downforce and steadier handling, especially through the fast, sweeping corners you’ll see this weekend. In short, it should translate into better grip and a stronger push on the straights without the team having to change their driving style.
Alpine F1 Team: Alpine F1 Team did not submit any updates for this event.
Cadillac: Cadillac has tweaked the front‑corner brake cooling – the little air scoop and its exit are now reshaped for better airflow. That means the brakes stay cooler, so drivers can brake later and harder without worrying about fade. In short, the car will be more reliable through the high‑speed corners and can attack the track with confidence all weekend.
